The Product Backlog is constantly updated with the most recent information.
The Product Backlog is only updated during a release planning meeting, with the stakeholders and the change control board present.
Product Backlog items must be sized so that the most important items are no larger than one Sprint.
Product Backlog items must not exceed 8 work points, which is the average of the acceptable size range of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 13.

question: What are the Developers accountable for?

answers.text: Creating a plan for the Sprint: the Sprint Backlog.
Organizing the work needed to achieve the Sprint Goal.
Selecting the Product Owner.
Reporting on their productivity.

question: True or False: When several teams work on the same product, each Scrum Team must have its own Product Owner.

answers.text: True
False

question: In the middle of the Sprint, the customer decides she wants two new features. The Product Owner could:

answers.text: Add these features to the Product Backlog.
Present these features at the next Daily Scrum.
Ask the Developers to consider whether they can add these features to the current Sprint without putting the Sprint Goal at risk.
Ask the Scrum Master to add these features to the current Sprint.

question: When should the Product Owner take part in the Daily Scrum?

answers.text: When the Product Owner needs to represent the stakeholders' point of view to the Developers.
When there are impediments to discuss.
When the Scrum Master asks the Product Owner to attend the event.
When the Product Owner is actively working on Sprint Backlog items; he or she then takes part as a Developer.

question: An organization has decided to adopt Scrum, but management wants to change the terminology to fit the terminology already used. What is likely to happen?

answers.text: Without a new vocabulary as a reminder of the change, very little change may actually happen.
The organization may not understand what has changed within Scrum, and thereby lose the benefits of the framework.
Management may feel less anxious.
All of these answers are plausible.

question: True or False: Cross-functional teams are optimized to work on a single component or a single layer of a system.

answers.text: True
False

question: What are three benefits, for a Product Owner, of sharing a clearly defined Product Goal with the Scrum Team?

answers.text: It is not mandatory in Scrum, so there is no real benefit.
It provides overall direction, which makes Sprints feel less like isolated pieces of work.
It makes it easier to inspect incremental progress at the Sprint Review.
It helps the Developers estimate the date on which the Product Backlog will be finished.
It helps the Scrum Team stay focused and evaluate every decision against the Product Goal.

question: Which three things should a Product Owner focus on to make sure the product delivers value?

answers.text: Direct customer feedback.
Minimizing changes to the product scope.
Velocity increasing over time.
The extent to which the product features are actually used.
How quickly and easily the product can be adopted and used by its customers.

question: True or False: At the Sprint Review, the role of the stakeholders is to reorder the Product Backlog.

answers.text: True
False

question: Which of the following are criteria for ordering Product Backlog items?

answers.text: How relevant they are to achieving the Product Goal.
The value of the Product Backlog items.
Dependencies between Product Backlog items.
The number of stakeholders who approve the item.
The Scrum Master's availability.

question: All Scrum artifacts must be transparent to ensure sufficiently accurate inspection. What are two measures that ensure the transparency of the Product Backlog?

answers.text: The Product Backlog is accessible to all stakeholders.
The Product Backlog only contains work for the next 2 Sprints.
The Product Backlog is managed using a web-based tool.
Every Product Backlog item has a MoSCoW priority.
The Product Backlog is ordered.

question: How much work is required of the Developers to complete a Product Backlog item selected during Sprint Planning?

answers.text: As much work as possible during the Sprint, with the remainder carried over to the next Sprint.
Time split proportionally between analysis, design, development and testing.
All of the development work and at least some of the testing.
As much as is needed to meet the Scrum Team's Definition of Done.

question: You are the Scrum Master of four Scrum Teams working from the same Product Backlog. Several Developers come to you to complain: the work identified for the next two Sprints will require the full-time involvement of a specialist from outside the Scrum Teams. What should the Scrum Master take into account when deciding how to proceed?

answers.text: The desire to maintain a stable velocity.
The benefit of letting the Developers work out a solution themselves.
The need to have enough work to keep all the Developers busy.
The ability of the Scrum Teams to produce integrated Increments.

question: A new Developer keeps running into conflicts with the other members of the Scrum Team, which is affecting the delivery of the Increment. If necessary, who is responsible for removing this Developer from the Scrum Team?

answers.text: The hiring manager, since he or she hired the Developer.
The Product Owner, since he or she controls the return on investment (ROI).
The Scrum Team, as it is self-managing.
The Scrum Master, since he or she is responsible for removing impediments.

question: How much time is there after a Sprint to prepare for the next one?

answers.text: The break between Sprints is limited to one week for a one-month Sprint, and usually less for shorter Sprints.
Enough time to determine and document the requirements for the next Sprint.
Enough time for the Developers to finish testing the previous Sprint's work.
None. A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
All of the above are allowed, depending on the situation.

question: What is the Product Owner's role in defining the Sprint Goal?

answers.text: The Product Owner cannot attend Sprint Planning without having documented the Sprint Goal beforehand.
The Product Owner defines the scope of a Sprint and therefore also the Sprint Goal.
The Product Owner should come to Sprint Planning with a business objective in mind and collaborate with the Developers to craft the Sprint Goal.
The Product Owner is not accountable for the Sprint Goal; that accountability lies solely with the Developers.
The Product Owner must collaborate with the stakeholders to define the goal of each Sprint.

question: What outcome can be expected from a Scrum Team as it matures?

answers.text: A Scrum Master is no longer needed, since it is now a mature team.
It will expand its Definition of Done to include more stringent criteria.
Time-boxing the Sprint will no longer be necessary.
Sprint Reviews will no longer be necessary.
Sprint Retrospectives will now last more than 4 hours.

question: The Developers ask their Product Owner to reorder the Product Backlog. The team is waiting for a component to be delivered by an external supplier: without that component, the next Sprint will not keep the whole team busy. As the Scrum Master, what advice would you give the Product Owner?

answers.text: Ask him or her to reorder the Product Backlog so that the work involving the external component can be planned into a separate Sprint.
Tell him or her that the Product Backlog must be ordered so as to optimize how busy the Developers are.
Remind him or her that the main concern is the flow of value reflected by the order of the Product Backlog.

question: True or False: The Product Owner must define clear and unambiguous acceptance criteria for every Product Backlog item before it can be selected during Sprint Planning.

answers.text: True
False

question: After several Sprints, the Product Owner tells the Scrum Master that a key stakeholder has just started using the product. That stakeholder is unhappy with its quality, and the Product Owner shares that opinion. How should the Scrum Master respond?

answers.text: Encourage the Product Owner to include quality requirements in the Product Backlog and to communicate the stakeholders' concerns to the Developers.
Pass the concern on to the testers so that the way the product is verified can be improved.
Collaborate with the Product Owner to understand the desired solution and help shape an approach for raising the issue with the Developers.
Tell the Product Owner that the issue has been noted and will be addressed at the Sprint Retrospective.
Explain to the Product Owner that it is up to the Developers alone to define acceptable quality standards.

question: The Product Owner is the person accountable if a product fails to meet its objectives or does not create value. Does this mean the Product Owner has the final say on the Definition of Done?

answers.text: Yes, the Product Owner defines the Definition of Done. The Developers may be consulted.
No, the Scrum Team defines the Definition of Done, unless it is part of the organizational standards. The Product Owner is just one member of the Scrum Team.

question: Which of the following practices can help the Product Owner minimize waste when building and maintaining the Product Backlog?

answers.text: Avoid distracting the Scrum Team by keeping new items in a separate Product Backlog until they are fully understood.
Transfer responsibility for the Product Backlog to somebody else.
Only describe Product Backlog items in detail when it seems likely that they will be implemented.
Remove Product Backlog items that have not been worked on for a long time.

question: A project manager in your organization has raised concerns about product progress and the money being spent. What are the two best responses?

answers.text: Share the latest stakeholder briefing document prepared by the Product Owner.
Show him or her the earned value analysis (EVA) report.
Scrum has no project managers, so their concerns should be ignored.
Talk with the project manager and share the current impediments as well as the forecast for the Sprint.
Promote transparency by sharing the Product Backlog and making sure the project manager has access to it.

question: True or False: The Sprint Review is an opportunity to gather feedback from the stakeholders.

answers.text: True
False

question: Which of the following are feedback loops in Scrum?

answers.text: The Sprint Review.
Release planning.
The Sprint Retrospective.
The Daily Scrum.
The refinement meeting.

question: A Product Backlog is:

answers.text: Managed by the Product Owner.
Visible only to the Product Owner and the stakeholders.
Ordered by value, dependencies and risk.
An exhaustive list of pre-approved requirements to be implemented.
An inventory of the work remaining to be done for the product.

question: True or False: A Product Owner overseeing several teams working on the same product must maintain a separate Product Backlog for each team.

answers.text: True
False

question: What can the "cone of uncertainty" be used for?

answers.text: To determine whether quality should be reduced, in line with the "iron triangle" of project management.
To determine the cost of a project before it starts.
To determine the length of the next Sprint.
To illustrate that the further out a forecast reaches, the less certain it is.
